name: Poincaré Dodecahedral Universe
description: A closed Friedmann universe whose space is a dodecahedron with each face glued to the face opposite it after a tenth of a turn, the 3-sphere divided by the binary icosahedral group. Every local measurement agrees with Friedmann's, and space is 120 times smaller than the 3-sphere of the same curvature. Jean-Pierre Luminet, Jeffrey R. Weeks, Alain Riazuelo, Roland Lehoucq, and Jean-Philippe Uzan proposed it in 2003 for the weak correlations of the microwave background at wide angles.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the scale factor $a$ is the radius of curvature of space, a length. Space is the 3-sphere with the points $p$ and $hp$ identified for every map $h$ in $I^*$, and $I^*$ is the binary icosahedral group, 120 rotations of the 3-sphere that move every point but the identity. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: The microwave sky mapped by the WMAP satellite in its first year was too quiet at wide angles [luminet2003]. Its quadrupole, the largest pattern that can be measured, came in at about a seventh of the strength expected in an infinite flat universe, and the correlations of temperature between two directions faded to nothing once the directions were more than 60° apart [luminet2003]. Jean-Pierre Luminet, Jeffrey R. Weeks, Alain Riazuelo, Roland Lehoucq, and Jean-Philippe Uzan took the quiet to mean that space is too small to hold the longest waves: "Just as the vibrations of a bell cannot be larger than the bell itself, the density fluctuations in space cannot be larger than space itself" [luminet2003]. Their proposal, in October 2003, was a block of space shaped like a dodecahedron with each face glued to the face opposite it, so that whatever leaves through one face comes back in through the other [luminet2003]. From inside, looking out through a face, "we have the illusion of looking into an adjacent copy of the dodecahedron" [luminet2003].¶Twelve pentagons drawn on a globe cover it snugly when every corner angle is exactly 120° [luminet2003]. Gluing the faces of a dodecahedron brings its 30 edges together in ten groups of three, so the angle between two faces along an edge has to be exactly 120°, and in a Euclidean dodecahedron it is about 117° [luminet2003]. A dodecahedron drawn on the 3-sphere, the space of positive curvature, has edge angles of exactly 120°, and 120 such dodecahedra tile the 3-sphere as the twelve pentagons tile the globe [luminet2003]. Space is then positively curved and finite, with a volume 120 times smaller than that of the whole 3-sphere of the same radius of curvature [luminet2003]. Each face meets its partner after a turn of a tenth of a circle, and the 120 motions of the 3-sphere that carry one dodecahedron onto each of the others form the binary icosahedral group, none of them but the identity leaving any point where it was [lachiezerey1995, aurich2005]. Topologists know the result as the Poincaré dodecahedral space, and its nickname is the soccer ball universe [aurich2005, key2007].¶The same 120 cells had turned up in cosmology in 1980, in J. Richard Gott III's survey of the closed universes whose space is a 3-sphere with points identified [gott1980]. He was after "cells that are small in all dimensions relative to the radius of curvature of the sphere", so that light could cross a cell early on [gott1980]. In the dodecahedral space the nearest image of an observer stands a tenth of the way round a great circle, at $\chi = \pi/5$ in units of the radius of curvature, and each cell fits inside a sphere of radius $0.388$ [gott1980]. No other way of identifying points of the 3-sphere makes the largest radius of a cell smaller [gott1980]. A closed universe can therefore be only so small, and Gott concluded that its radius "cannot be much smaller than its radius of curvature" [gott1980].¶That smallest cell is about the size of the visible universe [luminet2003]. With the density of the universe 1.3% above the density that makes space flat, $\Omega_0 \simeq 1.013$, the largest sphere inside a cell and the smallest sphere around it have radii of 0.31 and 0.39 of the radius of curvature, and the sphere of last scattering, the farthest surface in view, has a radius of 0.38 [luminet2003]. The octopole, the next pattern after the quadrupole, matched for $1.010 < \Omega_0 < 1.014$, and the quadrupole as well for $1.012 < \Omega_0 < 1.014$ [luminet2003]. Nothing else could be adjusted, since the gluing allows only a regular dodecahedron, and the space "offers no free parameters in its construction" [luminet2003]. It is globally homogeneous too, so its power spectrum is the same for every observer in it [luminet2003]. The 3-sphere vibrates at every whole wave number $\beta$, and the dodecahedral space at $\beta = 1$, the constant, and then only at 13, 21, 25, 31, and some odd numbers after, every odd one from 61 on and never an even one [aurich2005].¶Would the sky show the gluing directly? A space this small makes the sphere of last scattering cross its own images, in six pairs of circles of angular radius about 35°, laid out like the faces of a dodecahedron [luminet2003]. Neil J. Cornish, David N. Spergel, Glenn D. Starkman, and Eiichiro Komatsu searched the first year of WMAP's maps for pairs of circles back to back, found none of radius larger than 25°, and noted that the search excludes the dodecahedron with its circles of 35° [cornish2004]. Luminet's group had used only the vibrations of wave numbers 13, 21, and 25, 59 of them in all, and at the University of Ulm, Ralf Aurich, Sven Lustig, and Frank Steiner computed 10521, up to $\beta = 155$ [aurich2005]. With all of them the weak correlations at wide angles came out for $\Omega_{\rm tot}$ between 1.016 and 1.020, and the circles with radii of 40° to 50° [aurich2005]. The Doppler effect and the integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect blur the circles, so that "the signal of the six pairs of matched circles could be missed" [aurich2005].¶In Toruń and Warsaw, Boudewijn F. Roukema, Bartosz Lew, Magdalena Cechowska, Andrzej Marecki, and Stanislaw Bajtlik noticed how fast the circles shrink as the density falls: at $\Omega_{\rm tot} = 1.009$ their radius is nearly zero [roukema2004]. Searching the sky for small circles in the dodecahedral pattern, they found the strongest match at $11 \pm 1°$ with the faces turned 36° one way, and none with the faces turned the other way [roukema2004]. Three years later Joey Shapiro Key, Cornish, Spergel, and Starkman found the same peak at 11°, and saw it disappear once the mean temperature of each circle was taken out of the comparison [key2007]. With the maps filtered and the six pairs searched together, circles down to about 5° were within reach, and none turned up [key2007]. That, in their words, "effectively rules out the Poincaré Dodecahedral model as an interesting shape for the Universe" [key2007].

related.text: Friedmann's closed universe, $k = +1$, before any points are identified. Every local measurement agrees with Friedmann's, and the dodecahedral universe holds a hundred and twentieth of its volume [luminet2003].
Einstein's closed universe of 1917, whose space is the whole 3-sphere held at one radius. The dodecahedral universe cuts the same 3-sphere into 120 dodecahedra and keeps one of them [luminet2003].
Friedmann universes made finite by identifying points of flat or hyperbolic space. Space here is closed already, and identifying its points makes it 120 times smaller [luminet2003].

The closed universe with nothing in it but a positive cosmological constant, $a = \ell\cosh(ct/\ell)$, is de Sitter space. With points of its space identified under the same group it is a dodecahedral universe that never stops expanding.

De Sitter space with each event identified with its antipode, an older universe made by identifying points. There the identification reverses time, and here it moves points of space within one moment.

coordinates.name: Comoving
domains: (t, p) \sim (t, h p) \;\text{for every } h \in I^*

parameters.description: Scale factor ($a > 0$), a length, the radius of curvature of space at the time $t$; the volume of space is $\pi^2a^3/60$

coordinates.convention: We use cosmic time $t$ and the angles $(\chi, \theta, \phi)$ of the unit 3-sphere about one observer, with $a\chi$ the distance from that observer. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, a prime is $a' = da/d(ct)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Conformal Time
domains: (\eta, p) \sim (\eta, h p) \;\text{for every } h \in I^*

parameters.description: Scale factor ($a > 0$), a length, the radius of curvature of space at the conformal time $\eta$

coordinates.convention: We use the conformal time $\eta$, a pure number with $a\,d\eta = c\,dt$, and the angles $(\chi, \theta, \phi)$ of the unit 3-sphere about one observer. A prime is $a' = da/d\eta$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Toroidal
domains: (t, v, \alpha, \gamma) \sim (t, v, \alpha + \pi/5, \gamma + \pi/5) \;\text{and the other images under } I^*

parameters.description: Scale factor ($a > 0$), a length, the radius of curvature of space at the time $t$

coordinates.convention: We use cosmic time $t$ and the coordinates $(v, \alpha, \gamma)$ of the unit 3-sphere at the point $(\sqrt{1 - 2v}\cos\alpha, \sqrt{2v}\cos\gamma, \sqrt{2v}\sin\gamma, \sqrt{1 - 2v}\sin\alpha)$ of $\mathbb{R}^4$, in which a shift of $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ together is a Clifford translation. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, a prime is $a' = da/d(ct)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
